newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ahern set to form minority govt after Irish poll.
newsitem.headline: Ahern set to form minority govt after Irish poll.

text.p: Opposition Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern began preparations to form a minority government on Monday after his centre-right alliance won a cliffhanger poll.

"Cutting taxes, cutting crime and Northern Ireland will be my government's top priorities," Ahern told reporters as his party and its Progressive Democrats ally defeated Prime Minister John Bruton's centre-left "Rainbow Coalition."
Ahern, 45, is expected to be elected Ireland's youngest Prime Minister when parliament reconvenes on June 26 but will need the support of Independents to command a majority in parliament.
Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats needed 83 seats for a bare majority - the outgoing government held 85 - because the speaker of parliament is traditionally neutral.
But it managed only 81 after Mary Harney's Progressive Democrats were mauled at the polls for advocating cutting 25,000 civil service jobs and making single mothers stay at the parental home.
Harney's party won only four seats against eight in the previous parliamentt, weakening her case for getting one of the two top portfolios of Finance or Foreign affairs, political sources said.

The result ended a 30-month alliance between Bruton's Christian Democrat Fine Gael and the left-wing Labour and Democratic Left groupings which oversaw an economic boom which created 1,000 jobs a week.

Financial analysts said a minority government would cause some uncertainty but market sentiment would be dominated by domestic currency concerns and worries about a possible delay to Europe's economic and monetary union.
Seven Independents were elected, including many sympathetic to or with origins in Fianna Fail but with local agenda which Ahern would have to back in return for their support.
Ahern ruled out any immediate survival pact with Sinn Fein, the political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland.
The party won a seat in the border county of Monaghan and will occupy it after ending a boycott in 1986. It has failed in previous attempts to win a seat in the Dublin assembly.

Ahern urged the IRA to call a new truce to its war against British rule of Northern Ireland and said that such a move would breathe fresh life into Northern Ireland peace talks, from which Sinn Fein is barred because of the IRA campaign.
Fianna Fail pledged to cut the top rate of tax from 48 to 43 percent over five years and to launch a crackdown on all kinds of crime but with drugs trafficking its major target.
Ahern, like Bruton, is an enthusiastic advocate of Ireland being among the first wave of countries to join the euro single currency project.
Harney was less committed and had argued that Ireland should wait until Britain, its biggest trading partner, joins but her arguments will carry little weight, the sources said.
The election appeared to put a question mark over the career of one of Ireland's best-known international figures, Foreign Minister and Labour party leader Dick Spring.

His party's fortunes slumped. It won only 17 seats against 32 in the previous 1992 election, prompting speculation that Spring would step down as party leader and take a job either with the European Union or United Nations.
"I will stay on as long as people want me to stay on," Spring told reporters after he was re-elected in the southern country of Kerry.
The shape and make-up of Ahern's government will not be known in full until parliament resumes on June 23 to formally elect him Taoiseach (Prime Minister).
Harney had hoped for either the Finance Ministry or Foreign Affairs department but would have to settle for less, the sources said.
Fianna Fail sources said the job of Finance Minister was likely to be awarded the combative and vocal foe of excessive government spending, Charlie McCreevy.
The Foreign Minister's job was said to be the ambition of Fianna Fail stalwart Mary O'Rourke, whose brother, Brian Lenehan, is a former Foreign Minister.
